points: A data structure provides the concrete implementation that fulfills the interface’s specification.
A data structure provides the concrete representation of the stored data, turning the abstract specification into an actual layout.
Storing data alone is trivial – you can just dump it into a file – but the interesting part is defining operations on that data.
An interface lists the operations that are supported and describes what each operation does.
The data structure supplies the algorithms that implement those operations efficiently.
The course will concentrate on two primary interfaces and their special cases, emphasizing the separation of what to do from how to do it.
The same problem can be solved by many different data structures, each offering distinct trade‑offs.
Different data structures have different advantages; some operations are faster on one than on another.
Thus you choose a data structure based on which operations you need to be fast.
The two primary abstract data types we’ll study are the set and the sequence.
Python lists can store a sequence and preserve order, with items indexed as first, second, last.
We will focus on the sequence data structure today, and later mention the set interface.
Sequences and sets are closely related abstractly, but we will concentrate on sequences in the next lectures.
The class is Introduction to Algorithms, taught by Jason Ku with co‑instructors Eric Domen and Justin Solomon.
Jason will give the first lecture; the other two instructors will each give the next lecture.
The course focuses on algorithms and on solving computational problems.
Communication of ideas, not just code, is repeatedly stressed.
The class aims to prove solutions are correct and better, and to convey that to others.
A computational problem is a binary relation between a set of inputs and a set of outputs, where for each input we specify which outputs are correct.
The lecturer emphasizes that a computational problem is not just a trivial question but something you want to compute, possibly abstractly.
Inputs are the possible data the algorithm can receive; outputs are the possible results the algorithm can produce.

Today's agenda: brief administrative/course information followed by a high‑level discussion of what computation is.
We'll dive into Python basics, covering mathematical operations you can do with Python.
All slides containing code will be posted before lecture; download them in advance.
Class exercises will be on the slides; have the slides open while working through them.
Take notes on the code shown in class for future reference.
Read problem sets (P‑sets) as soon as they appear so terminology sinks in and you can connect lecture material to them.
Don't be afraid to just type some stuff in and see what it does.
Three big things we want you to get out of this course: knowledge of concepts, programming skills, and problem‑solving via P‑sets.
First goal: acquire knowledge of concepts, the theoretical foundation common to any class.
Second goal: develop programming skills through hands‑on coding.
Learning how to program involves figuring out what objects to create.
